newsitem.title: ITALY: Desecrated Jewish graves reconsecrated in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Desecrated Jewish graves reconsecrated in Italy.

text.p: Italian leaders and former resistance fighters joined some 150 Jews on Friday for a ceremony to reconsecrate Jewish graves desecrated by suspected neo-Nazis.

Interior Minister Giorgio Napolitano, police chief Fernando Masone and Rome's mayor Francesco Rutelli were among participants at the service at the Prima Porta cemetery on the northern outskirts of Rome.
Fourteen Jewish graves were desecrated on Sunday. Several of the tombstones were broken or had names and the Star of David ripped off in an attack that has shocked Italy.

One tomb was surrounded with barbed wire and swastikas with the German words "Arbeit Macht Frei" (Work Brings Freedom). The same words hung over the entrance to the Auschwitz death camp in Poland where millions of Jews died during World War Two.
Napolitano said his presence underlined Italy's commitment to hunt down the racists suspected of the attack.
"We have to ensure that fanatical anti-Semites are put in a position where they can do no more harm," he said.
Friday's ceremony took place on the 42nd anniversary of a deportation of Rome Jews to Nazi death camps in World War Two.
Veteran anti-fascist partisans were also at the service, after which relatives of the dead, some in tears, placed flowers on the restored graves.
Jewish community leader Tullia Zevi said the attack represented an offence not only to Jews but to all society.
"There must be widespread vigilance first of all and (an attempt) to identify who is inspiring these groups," she told Reuters.
"On the other hand, it is fundamental to pursue the education of the younger generation. They must be taught what happened in Europe 50 years ago," Zevi said.
The Vatican on Monday joined in condemnation of the attack while Jewish leaders said they were worried about growing anti-Semitism in Italy.

Shimon Samuels, director for international affairs for the Los Angeles-based Simon Wiesenthal Centre, said he was worried the unresolved war crimes case of former SS captain Erich Priebke could help provoke skinheads sympathetic to his cause.
"The longer this case is unresolved, the more likely it is that measures against the dead will escalate into atrocities against the living," Samuels said this week.

Priebke is in jail pending a decision by Italy's highest court on how to proceed in a new trial against him for his role in the World War Two massacre of 335 men and boys at the Ardeatine Caves south of Rome.
A first trial ended in uproar in August when a court found him guilty but not liable for punishment.
